title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used the hosted model gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, contamination‑check evidence (preregistered 10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks with zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of operator intent into network device configurations using generative language models promises productivity gains but risks generating incorrect or unsafe changes that can produce outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore integrates model generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so that unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness.

We designed and preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? To isolate the marginal effect of validator+repair, the adapter enforced shared‑initial generation semantics so the same initial LLM candidate was scored under both conditions. Our contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) with shared‑initial semantics; (2) a fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome with operational interpretation and reproducibility notes.
sections.related_work:
LLMs produce factual errors and show prompt sensitivity across domains; mitigation approaches include grounding (retrieval), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded agent architectures [https://openalex.org/W4399803256, https://openalex.org/W4410125989]. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies [https://openalex.org/W4399629579, https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Architectural proposals combine LLM generation with deterministic validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops to improve safety; empirical red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies document tool‑description injection and cross‑tool ambiguity as practical risks [10.2139/ssrn.7203631, 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10646209/v1]. Surveys and meta‑evaluations call for externally auditable, preregistered measurements to isolate marginal effects of safety interventions; our preregistered paired estimand responds directly to that methodological gap [https://openalex.org/W4411523078, https://openalex.org/W4411735779].

Distinct from broad benchmarking work that compares models on held‑out questions, our study isolates the marginal operational effect of adding a deterministic validator+repair to a fixed model and fixed generation policy (shared initial candidate), thereby addressing an underexplored question in GVR evaluation: under what baseline failure prevalence conditions does automated repair provide measurable marginal benefit?
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary inferential plan. The study was preregistered (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) as a paired confirmatory test with n = 200 tasks, a single pre‑registered primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and a model‑call cap of 400 (one initial generation per task plus at most one repair call if validation failed). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; exact McNemar was used for hypothesis testing and 95% CIs were computed by bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and a target 50% relative reduction; these assumptions were frozen before execution.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and target states plus workflow constraints (examples: make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields) and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces the task‑encoded intent/constraint rules and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the contamination artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) records zero disagreement flags for the executed holdout. We note and disclose that the explicit labeled random seed used to select the Mininet holdout is absent from the archived bundle (a known reproducibility gap), but the contamination summary confirms the detector executed and reported zero disagreements.

Adapter enforcement, shared‑initial semantics, and model configuration. To isolate the effect of validator+repair, the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single deterministic initial candidate was produced and reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This removes per‑condition sampling variance and isolates repair effects on the same generator output. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider label openai_responses) invoked under adapter accounting shown in deterministic_reconciliation: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}. Model configuration artifact (execution/model_configuration.json) records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and maximum_attempts_per_call = 1. Planned repair policy: if the primary validator reported violations, issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; up to 200 repair calls were allowed but conditional on initial validation failures.

Execution accounting, missingness, and contamination handling. The preregistration established deterministic exclusion rules: pairs with mutual infrastructure failures would be excluded and logged; tasks flagged for primary validator vs emulator disagreement were to be excluded from the primary analysis and subject to sensitivity analyses. These rules were applied deterministically during execution; the missingness and contamination artifacts show complete_pairs = 200 and no contamination flags. All executed model calls, prompt texts, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were archived in the execution manifest and analysis bundle.
sections.results:
Execution summary and contingency counts. The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400 (shared initial reused across conditions), completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar (two‑sided) yields p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity, cost accounting, and provider audit. Because every initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. Provider accounting artifacts (deterministic_reconciliation.json) record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, confirming one generator invocation per task reused across conditions.

Representative diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (e.g., pair-000001 … pair-000006) show that shared initial generator outputs matched the required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each representative record. Difficulty annotations in the validator traces (patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) verify tasks exercised nontrivial workflow constraints despite producing validator‑satisfying candidates. The Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and the contamination summary artifact reports zero validator–emulator disagreements.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation of a degenerate confirmatory outcome. The outcome—zero baseline validator failures—illustrates a simple logical fact: when a chosen model, prompt policy, and deterministic adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for every item in a workload, an additional validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This does not imply GVR is never useful; rather, it demonstrates that GVR’s measurable marginal benefit depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage.

Artifact‑grounded explanations for zero baseline failures. The archived artifacts support several concrete, nonexclusive explanations: (1) the prompt template together with deterministic sampling produced candidates that conformed to the explicit task‑bank constraints (shared initial responses match reference sequences in representative artifacts); (2) the curated task bank encodes explicit required_sequences that map directly to deterministic validator checks, likely making these tasks amenable to a constrained generator/prompting policy; and (3) the single repair budget and shared_initial design remove per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway to produce alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational recommendations. Practitioners should instrument workload‑level baseline failure prevalence before investing heavily in automated repair automation. Where baseline validator failures are low, resources often yield higher marginal returns by improving validator fidelity (richer device semantics, multi‑vendor models), expanding adversarial testing, or enabling multi‑sample/multi‑model generation policies that increase candidate diversity. Conversely, when baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with an appropriate repair budget and targeted repair prompts can reduce validator‑detected errors; those gains remain conditional on validator completeness and repair effectiveness.

Contamination, reproducibility, and the known seed gap. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero disagreements; this provides evidence that primary validator verdicts were not contradicted by the holdout emulator on the sampled subset. We transparently report a reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact recording the randomized holdout selection seed is absent from the archived bundle, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the specific holdout composition despite the contamination summary evidence. This gap is documented in the Disclosure and in the reproducibility notes and does not change the observed zero‑disagreement outcome for the executed holdout.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This artifact‑grounded null result emphasizes that measured marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, improve validator fidelity with richer emulator or device semantics, explore multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and test multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
